title: Demand forecasting for franchise networks: a practical guide
summary: Demand forecasting for franchise networks starts from outlet sales, not warehouse orders. Across 64 outlets, pooled demand is 8 times steadier than in one.
body_markdown:
**By Elie Dufeu, CTO & Co-Founder, Metreecs.** Published 23 November 2026.


Demand forecasting for franchise networks predicts what each outlet will sell, product by product, and shares that single forecast between the franchisor that buys the stock and the franchisees that order it. It works when the forecast is built from outlet sales, and it goes wrong when the franchisor reads franchisee orders as demand.


A franchise has a planning problem that an owned chain does not have. The franchisor negotiates with suppliers and fills a warehouse, while dozens of independent owners decide every week how much to order and carry the stock on their own books. Two parties plan the same product with different numbers and different incentives.


This guide covers what makes franchise demand forecasting different, how to build one forecast that both sides use, how to turn it into an order proposal for each outlet, and what to do with an outlet that has no history. It follows one illustrative network, a pet supplies franchise with 64 outlets, and the arithmetic is our own. If you would rather look at your own outlets, you can[review your network's order data with our team](https://www.metreecs.com/form/discover) .


**Key Takeaways**


- US franchising is projected to grow from 832,521 to 845,000 establishments in 2026, with $921.4 billion in output (International Franchise Association). Each of those units places its own orders.
- France counted 2,035 franchise networks and 93,395 franchised outlets in 2025, for €93.71 billion in revenue (Fédération française de la franchise). Food retail and fast food made up 45.9% of that revenue, so more than half came from other sectors.
- Pooling steadies demand. If one outlet sells 20 units a week, give or take 6, then 64 independent outlets sell 1,280, give or take 48. Relative variation falls from 30% to 3.75%, which is 8 times lower.
- Orders are a poor stand-in for demand. In the worked example, franchisees who pad their orders by 25% during a shortage add 1,280 phantom units in four weeks, a full week of network sales.
- A new outlet can start from comparable outlets. At 55% of a mature volume of 20 units, the opening forecast is 11 units a week, and actual sales take over as the weeks accumulate.


## What is demand forecasting for franchise networks?


Demand forecasting for franchise networks estimates future customer demand for every product in every franchised outlet, then adds those estimates up to the regional and network levels. The franchisor uses the totals to buy from suppliers and to stock its warehouse. Each franchisee uses the outlet figures to place orders.


The forecast therefore lives at three levels at once. A franchisee needs it by product and by week for one outlet, or by day for fresh goods. A regional manager needs outlet totals, and the purchasing team needs one network figure per product. A coherent forecast gives the same answer whichever way you add it up.


Franchising reaches well beyond restaurants. The Fédération française de la franchise counted 2,035 networks and 93,395 franchised outlets in France in 2025, with €93.71 billion in revenue. Food retail accounted for 33.8% of that revenue and fast food for 12.1%, which leaves more than half to home equipment, car services, personal care, and other retail.


Demand forecasting for franchise networks therefore has to work for that wider group: a pet store, an optician, a garden center, or a bakery. Perishable products add shelf life to the problem, and we cover that case in the guide to[food demand forecasting for perishable inventory](https://www.metreecs.com/blog/food-demand-forecasting) .


## Why franchise demand forecasting differs from an owned chain


The statistics behind demand forecasting for franchise networks are the same as in any retail chain. What changes is who owns the stock, who holds the data, and who places the order.


### The franchisee owns the stock and places the order


In most franchise agreements, the franchisee buys the goods and owns them once they are delivered. A central planner in an owned chain can push stock to a store. A franchisor can usually only propose a quantity, and the owner accepts it or changes it.


A franchise forecast therefore has to be explainable. An owner who pays for every unsold unit will follow a number only if they can see what it is based on: last year's sales, the promotion planned for next week, the weather effect on that product.


### The franchisor sees orders, and demand sits in the tills


The franchisor's enterprise resource planning (ERP) system records what the warehouse shipped to each outlet. That is sell-in. What customers bought, the sell-out, sits in the point-of-sale (POS) system of each outlet.


Many networks already collect outlet revenue to calculate royalties, usually as one total per day or per month. Forecasting needs the same feed by product. One mistake we repeatedly see is a network forecast built on warehouse shipments, simply because that is the data the franchisor already holds.


### Outlets differ more than company stores


Franchised outlets vary in floor area, catchment, opening hours, and local range. Some owners run one outlet and others run ten. One outlet has eight years of history and its neighbor opened in the spring.


A single network average hides all of this. In the pet supplies example, the average outlet sells 20 bags a week of the best-selling 12 kg dog food, but individual outlets range from 6 to 45. An order guide based on the average overstocks the small outlet and starves the large one.


### Two profit and loss accounts


The franchisor earns royalties on sales and often a margin on the goods it supplies. The franchisee pays for unsold stock out of their own cash. A stockout hurts both, while overstock mostly hurts the franchisee.


That asymmetry explains a lot of ordering behavior. An owner who has been left with dead stock after a pushed promotion will order below every later proposal. A shared forecast only gets used when both sides believe it serves both accounts.


## Build one franchise network forecast from sales, not orders


The inputs to demand forecasting for franchise networks are outlet sales by product and day, stock levels, and a calendar of promotions and range changes. The output is one forecast per product and outlet that adds up to the network figure.


### Start at the outlet and reconcile upward


Outlet-level demand is noisy, and network-level demand is steady. Take the 12 kg dog food bag. One outlet sells 20 bags a week with a standard deviation of 6, which is a relative variation of 30%.


Add 64 outlets that vary independently, and the mean becomes 1,280 bags while the standard deviation becomes 6 × √64 = 48. Relative variation drops to 3.75%, 8 times lower than in one outlet. Real outlets move together in part (the same promotion, the same cold week), so the true gain is smaller, but the direction holds.


Good forecasting uses both levels. The network and the region carry the seasonal shape and the promotion effect, because the signal is clean there. The outlet carries its own share of the total and its local pattern.


The M5 forecasting competition was built on this structure. Its organizers, Makridakis, Spiliotis, and Assimakopoulos, asked participants to forecast 30,490 product-store series from a large US retailer, which summed up into 42,840 series across store, state, category, and total levels. Forecasts at the bottom had to add up to every level above, which is the same requirement a franchisor and its franchisees have.


For slow products, a single outlet may sell one or two units a week, with many weeks at zero. Those series need methods designed for sparse sales, described in our article on[intermittent demand forecasting](https://www.metreecs.com/blog/intermittent-demand-forecasting) . A model trained across all outlets also lets a small outlet borrow the seasonal curve it could never estimate alone.


### Why orders mislead


Lee, Padmanabhan, and Whang described the problem in 1997 in Sloan Management Review: orders vary more than sales as they move up a supply chain. One of the causes they named is shortage gaming, where buyers inflate orders when supply is rationed.


Ines owns three outlets in the pet supplies network. In March, a supplier delay leaves the franchisor's warehouse short of the 12 kg bag, and it ships 80% of every order. Ines reacts as most owners would and orders 25% more the following week, to receive what she actually needs.


When every owner does the same, the 64 outlets order 1,600 bags a week against customer sales of 1,280. Over four weeks, that is 1,280 phantom bags, a full week of network sales. A forecast built on orders tells the franchisor to buy that extra week of stock just as supply recovers.


Then the owners stop padding and order below sales to use up what they hold. The warehouse is left with stock nobody ordered for real, and the order history shows a spike and a dip that customers never produced. The same four weeks read from POS data show flat demand.


Raw sales have their own flaw. While an outlet is out of stock, it sells nothing, and the till records zero where demand existed. The forecast input should be sales corrected for out-of-stock days, which means the stock record matters as much as the sales record.


### Three ways to forecast in a franchise


Approach Input data What it does well Where it falls short Fits


Each franchisee orders by feel The owner's memory and last week's sales Uses local knowledge No view of promotions or supply, padding during shortages Very small networks with a short range


Franchisor forecast from warehouse shipments Orders shipped to outlets Simple, the data is already in the ERP Reads padding and batching as demand, no outlet detail Purchasing totals for stable products


Shared forecast from outlet sales POS sales by product and day, stock, promotion calendar One number for both sides, an order proposal per outlet Needs a daily POS feed and clean product codes Networks from a few dozen outlets up


## Turn the forecast into an order proposal for each outlet


A forecast changes nothing until it becomes a quantity on an order form. The proposal is what the franchisee actually sees.


**Order proposal = forecast over the cover period + safety stock − stock on hand − stock in transit** , rounded to the pack or pallet layer.


The cover period is the time the order has to last. It runs from today until the delivery after this one arrives, so it equals the review period plus the lead time.


Camille is supply director at the pet supplies franchisor. She works through the 12 kg bag for one outlet in a mid-sized town that orders on Monday and is delivered on Thursday.


1. Cover period: 7 days between orders plus 3 days of lead time, so 10 days.
2. Forecast: 20 bags a week, which is about 29 bags over 10 days.
3. Safety stock: 8 bags, set from the outlet's forecast error on this product.
4. Stock on hand: 14 bags, with nothing in transit.
5. Proposal: 29 + 8 − 14 = 23 bags, rounded to 24 because the bags ship in layers of 6.


Before the proposal existed, that outlet ordered a flat 30 bags every Monday. Against sales of 20, that added 10 bags a week until the owner skipped an order. After four weeks the back room held 40 surplus bags, two weeks of sales, and at a purchase price of €38 that was €1,520 of the owner's cash in one product.


### Let the franchisee override, and keep the reason


The owner knows things the data does not: roadworks outside the door, a competitor opening nearby, a local dog show. The ordering screen should let them change the proposal and pick a reason from a short list.


Those overrides are worth measuring. Comparing the proposal, the final order, and the sales that followed shows which changes improved the result, a method we describe in the article on[forecast value add](https://www.metreecs.com/blog/forecast-value-add) . In our experience deploying outlet-level proposals, showing the calculation behind each quantity does as much for adoption as the accuracy of the forecast.


## Demand forecasting for new franchise outlets


Networks grow by opening outlets, and each opening starts with no sales history, which makes it the hardest case in franchise demand forecasting. The International Franchise Association projects 845,000 US franchise establishments in 2026, up from 832,521, which means about 12,500 net new units placing first orders.


Mateo signs for outlet 65 of the pet supplies network, in a town of 30,000 people. The franchisor's opening package is a standard list, the same for every new owner. A forecast based on comparable outlets sizes it for his catchment instead.


1. Pick five to eight comparable outlets, matched on catchment size, format, and floor area.
2. Build their ramp-up curve: sales in each week after opening as a share of their mature level.
3. Apply the curve to the mature volume of the comparables. They sell 20 bags a week at maturity and reached 55% in their first four weeks, so Mateo's opening forecast is 11 bags a week.
4. Blend in actual sales as they arrive, with a weight equal to weeks open ÷ (weeks open + 8).
5. Retire the comparables once the outlet has traded through a full year.


After six weeks, Mateo's outlet is averaging 14 bags a week, while the curve says 12 for that stage. The weight on his own sales is 6 ÷ 14 = 0.43. The blended forecast is 0.43 × 14 + 0.57 × 12 = 12.9, so about 13 bags a week.


The constant 8 is a tuning choice. A higher value trusts the comparables for longer, which suits products with erratic weekly sales. The same logic applies to products with no history, covered in our guide to[new product forecasting without sales history](https://www.metreecs.com/blog/new-product-forecasting-without-sales-history) .


## How to roll out demand forecasting for franchise networks


The order of the steps matters more than the model. Most of the early work in demand forecasting for franchise networks is data plumbing and agreement between the franchisor and the owners.


1. Get product-level sales from every POS, every day. Check what the franchise agreement says about data sharing, and map local product codes to the network catalog.
2. Record stock and out-of-stock days. Without them, sales understate demand for exactly the products that sell best.
3. Share one calendar. National promotions and range changes come from the franchisor, and owners add local events.
4. Forecast by product, outlet, and week, then reconcile. Outlet forecasts add up to the regional and network figures the purchasing team uses.
5. Publish the proposal where the owner orders. A number in a separate report gets ignored, and a pre-filled order line gets read.
6. Measure both sides. Track forecast error by outlet with weighted mean absolute percentage error (WMAPE), bias, the share of proposals accepted unchanged, availability, and stock cover.


Start with a pilot group of willing owners and the products that make most of the volume. Their results, in their own words, persuade other franchisees better than any head office presentation.


Many franchisors have no planning team to run this. A managed forecasting service is an alternative: the forecasts and proposals arrive ready to use, which is how Metreecs delivers[AI demand planning](https://www.metreecs.com/demand-planning) to networks without in-house data scientists.


## Where franchise forecasts break


Franchise demand forecasting runs into trouble in a few predictable places, and most of them have little to do with the model.


### Thin data in small outlets


An outlet that sells one unit a week of a product gives the model very little to learn from. Pooling across outlets helps, and safety stock still has to absorb the rest.


### Local events the data never sees


A street market or a road closure appears in no feed. The override with a reason code exists for this.


### Mixed tills and product codes


Franchisees often run different POS versions and create local items. Across Metreecs' work with franchise and multi-site operators, the first weeks of a rollout usually go to matching product codes between tills, well before any modeling.


### Trust between franchisor and owners


A forecast used to police owners stops receiving honest input. Li, Yang, and Yue (2023) modeled a brand and two franchisees in Production and Operations Management and found that sharing inventory between franchisees worked when the franchisor ran an internal market with clear trade rules and earned from royalties, with no extra margin on the traded goods. Coordination in a franchise depends on incentives as well as on numbers.


## FAQ


### How is demand forecasting for franchise networks different from forecasting for company-owned stores?


The models are similar, and the decision rights are different. In an owned chain, head office can allocate stock to stores. In a franchise, the owner buys and holds the stock, so the forecast reaches them as a proposal they can change, and it has to be explained.


### Should a franchisor forecast from franchisee orders or from outlet sales?


From outlet sales, corrected for out-of-stock days. Orders include padding during shortages, pack rounding, and each owner's habits, so they swing more than customer demand. Warehouse shipments remain useful as a check on the totals.


### How do you forecast demand for a franchise outlet that has just opened?


Use comparable outlets. Take their sales in the weeks after opening as a share of their mature level, apply that curve to the new outlet, and blend in actual sales as they arrive. After a full year, the outlet's own history is enough.


### Can a franchisor impose order quantities on franchisees?


It depends on the franchise agreement and on local law, so check both with counsel. In practice most networks propose quantities and let the owner adjust them, with minimums for the core range. A proposal that owners trust gets accepted far more often than one they are told to follow.


### Does demand forecasting for franchise networks only apply to food?


No. Any network where independent outlets order physical goods has the same structure: pet supplies, optical, home improvement, beauty, and car parts, among others. Food adds shelf life and daily ordering, which raises the stakes.


### How many outlets does a network need before a shared forecast pays off?


There is no fixed threshold. The gain from pooling grows with the number of outlets and the size of the range, and a few dozen outlets ordering several hundred products every week is already more than a spreadsheet can follow by hand.


## Conclusion


Demand forecasting for franchise networks comes down to one forecast built from outlet sales, read the same way by the franchisor and by every franchisee, and delivered as an order proposal the owner can accept or correct. Start with the daily sales feed and the stockout record, then bring new outlets in through comparable ones.
